 Why Reducing Risk, Not Counting It, Is the Right Security Metric
 By Eugene Dzihanau, Head of Cybersecurity Practice, EPAM Systems, Inc. 
 November 7, 2026 [ Join Cybersecurity Insiders ] 
 34 
 Security should not be measured by the number of vulnerabilities found. It should be measured by reductions in exploitable risk.
 That distinction matters because finding a risk and doing something about it are not the same accomplishment, even though security programs often get credit as if they were. Cloud security does not end with identifying risk. Organizations need the engineering capability to act on that intelligence across complex applications and infrastructure, addressing root causes rather than simply cataloging them, and moving forward with cloud and AI initiatives with more confidence as a result.
 The problem is that many organizations have become very good at finding risk without becoming equally good at eliminating it. Security teams can have more visibility than ever and still struggle to decide what deserves immediate attention and who owns fixing it.
 Closing that gap starts with understanding what’s at risk in the first place, and that means more than a list of vulnerabilities. It means a contextualized view of cloud assets, their configurations, how they relate to one another and the attack paths that connect them, across code, cloud, runtime, AI applications, SaaS and custom-hosted environments alike. A finding that looks minor in isolation can look very different once you understand it in the context of everything else it touches.
 Knowing About a Risk Isn’t the Same as Proving It Matters 
 Doing this well means being honest about which findings deserve attention. Identifying a vulnerability isn’t the same as proving it can be exploited, or containing an attack once someone has already exploited it. Not every flagged issue represents genuine, immediate risk and treating them all with equal urgency wastes remediation effort that should go toward what’s actually dangerous.
 One of the biggest mistakes organizations can make is equating a high severity score with immediate business risk. Context matters: where the vulnerability sits, what it connects to, whether an attacker can realistically exploit it and the business impact all influence what to fix first.
 That’s where dedicated offensive-security expertise earns its place in the process: bringing defensive, offensive and incident response experience to bear on a finding, testing it against real adversary tactics and techniques and helping teams distinguish potential exposure from the risks that genuinely require immediate engineering action. Without that validation step, security teams are left prioritizing by guesswork or severity score alone, neither of which reliably predicts what an attacker can do with a given weakness.
 The organizations that handle this well don’t treat remediation as a security-team-only responsibility. They connect security findings to the engineering teams that can address the underlying issue and set clear expectations for what gets fixed first.
 In practice, that discipline can come down to a few concrete habits:
 A single, prioritized risk register that ranks findings by validated exploitability and business impact, not just severity score, so remediation effort goes toward what matters first.
 Clear ownership for every open finding, assigned to the engineering team that can fix it, rather than left with a security team that can flag it but not resolve it.
 A remediation timeline tied to risk tier, so a critical, exploitable finding carries the same urgency as an outage.
 Regular review of aging findings, so unresolved issues don’t disappear into a backlog simply because they’ve been open for too long.
 These aren’t the only ways to operationalize risk reduction, but they represent the discipline. 
 Where Automation Actually Helps 
 Most of the attention AI has received in security has focused on detection. That’s useful, but it only addresses part of the problem. The more important question for security leaders isn’t whether AI can find another vulnerability. It’s whether AI can shorten the distance between identifying a meaningful risk and resolving it. That is what separates organizations that talk about closing the gap from those that actually close it.
 Automation’s more valuable role shows up later in the lifecycle: validating which paths across an organization’s external attack surface are exploitable, supporting root-cause remediation instead of one-off patches, and investigating runtime threats to assess their potential impact once something moves from theoretical exposure to a real incident. None of this is about generating more findings. It’s about helping organizations move more efficiently from risk evidence to corrective action, using what’s found not just to close individual tickets but to inform broader decisions about application modernization and cloud architecture.
 Multi-Cloud Adds Another Layer of Complexity 
 The challenge with multi-cloud isn’t simply that organizations have more environments to secure. Different cloud environments can involve different teams, tools and processes, making it harder to maintain a consistent view of what constitutes critical risk and what to address first.
 Enterprises increasingly run across multiple cloud providers (Google Cloud, AWS, Microsoft Azure and others) rather than just one. Running the same find–validate–fix loop across all of them, rather than treating each provider as a separate program is what lets an organization apply the same standard of risk reduction everywhere it runs, instead of only in the environment it happens to have invested in most.
 The Real Measure of Progress 
 The next evolution of cloud security will be less about how many risks an organization can surface and more about how quickly it can determine which risks matter and mobilize the right people and technology to eliminate them.
 The underlying point is simple. An organization’s security posture isn’t defined by how much risk it has found and cataloged. It’s defined by how much exploitable risk it has eliminated, how well it can distinguish real danger from noise and how consistently it can keep eliminating risk as new exposure appears across every environment it operates in.
